title: Modeling Requests, Latency, and Throughput

sections.title: Applying It to a Sizing Decision

html:
Modeling Requests, Latency, and Throughput

After the recommendation incident in Chapter 1, the engineers had to decide what to change before another rollout. Increasing the connection pool was one option. They could also reduce the time each lookup used a connection, serve more requests from a cache, or add application instances.

These changes have different costs. More instances give requests more workers, but each instance can also open another pool of database connections. A cache removes some reads from the database, provided the team decides what happens on a miss. Shorter connection occupancy lets the existing pool serve more lookups. The engineers had to know which resource was running out before choosing among them.

The engineers needed a model of how many operations each request creates and how long each operation occupies a constrained resource. A few rows of measured rates and durations often distinguish a workload that uses one-third of an allocation from one that approaches or exceeds its limit. Such estimates do not predict tail latency; bursts and variation require separate tests. When measured occupancy differs from the estimate, the engineers must investigate whether operations were counted incorrectly or whether their resource use changed under load.

Request Rates and Downstream Work

Think about what happens when a customer opens a product page. To them it is one action: they tapped a link and a page appeared. Behind it, the handler fetched the product, asked Recommendation Service for a list, and that service ran a database query of its own, each step holding a different resource for a different length of time. Counting page requests gives us the entry rate. To estimate the work at each dependency, we also need the calls created by the page handler.

Consider a proposed product-page path receiving 1,000 requests per second across the fleet. Forty percent use recommendations, so Recommendation Service receives approximately 400 lookups per second.

Suppose a cache supplies the result for 80 percent of those lookups. If every miss causes one database read, the database receives about 80 reads per second. If each recommendation lookup also checks three products through separate inventory calls, Inventory Service receives about 1,200 calls per second.

Downstream work created by one illustrative request path. All rates describe the fleet.
Operation Rate per second
Incoming product-page requests 1,000
Recommendation lookups 400
Database reads after cache misses 80
Individual inventory calls 1,200

A table of downstream operations per incoming request makes the handler’s workload assumptions explicit. If the three inventory checks are sent in one batch, there is one network call containing three items. The receiving service may still perform three database reads. The engineer sizing the HTTP client needs the call rate, while the engineer sizing the database needs the database-operation rate.

The estimate also assumes one database read per cache miss. Cache hit and miss counters cannot establish that relationship; the engineers must inspect the miss handler and count the database statements it executes. If assembling the record takes three queries, the 80 reads per second estimated here are really 240, and the comparison against the database’s limit changes with them. Retries have the same effect, since each additional attempt is another operation the database executes. Chapter 5 examines how caching reshapes this workload, including what the miss path does when the cache is empty.

Some work may happen after the page response. An analytics consumer, for example, can process an event later if the product requirement permits that delay. The page handler may still wait for the broker to acknowledge publication, but it does not wait for the consumer to finish.

That consumer has its own workload to support. Separating it from the page response changes when the work must finish, while its processing and storage requirements still need to be accounted for.

Average Concurrency

The multiplication we performed in Chapter 1 has a name and a notation worth adopting, because the notation is what lets us apply it to resources other than connection pools. Little’s Law states:

\[L = \lambda W.\]

Here, \(L\) is the average number of operations inside whatever we are measuring, \(\lambda\) is the rate passing through it, and \(W\) is the mean time each one spends there.

The reason this generalizes so freely is that the law makes almost no assumptions. It does not care about the arrival pattern, the service discipline, or the distribution of durations. It requires only a system whose contents are stable over the interval observed. A coffee shop makes that concrete: four customers arriving per minute, each staying five minutes, gives about twenty people inside. Narrow the boundary to the counter and \(W\) becomes the time at the counter alone, which is shorter, so \(L\) is smaller.

The same formula can describe a full request or a single stage of it, provided that arrival rate \(\lambda\) and mean duration \(W\) refer to the same boundary. Combining the request rate from one stage with the occupancy duration from another produces a misleading estimate.

Applying It to a Sizing Decision

Little’s Law converts a proposal into a concurrency estimate before the proposal is released. Suppose a team wants to add a tax-calculation call to checkout. Checkout runs at 180 requests per second across the fleet, the provider’s published median is 120 ms, and the client library defaults to a pool of 50 connections per instance across 6 instances.

Rearranged, the law answers three different questions from the same three quantities, and which one we rearrange for depends on what is fixed:

\[L = \lambda W \qquad \lambda = \frac{L}{W} \qquad W = \frac{L}{\lambda}.\]

Sizing the pool uses the first form: \(180 \times 0.120 = 21.6\) concurrent calls on average, about 3.6 per instance, so the default pool of 50 is far larger than the mean demand. Asking what the pool can sustain uses the second: 50 connections at 120 ms gives \(50 / 0.120 \approx 416\) calls per second per instance, well above the 30 each instance receives. Asking how slow the provider may become before the pool is the constraint uses the third: at 50 in use and 30 arrivals per second, \(W = 50/30 \approx 1.67\) seconds. So the pool absorbs a fourteenfold slowdown, and the deadline will stop the request long before the pool does.

The third calculation converts the pool limit into a latency threshold that can be monitored. Under these assumptions, the pool is not the binding constraint, so the team should evaluate the deadline and retry policy instead (Chapter 4).

Two limits apply to this estimate. The first is that these are averages over a stable interval, so they say nothing about the request that arrives when all 50 are briefly in use; Section \(\ref{sec:ch02-variation}\) takes up variability. The second is that \(\lambda\) must be the rate that actually reaches the resource. If 40 percent of checkouts are exempt from tax lookups, the rate is 108 per second rather than 180, and the estimate drops by the same proportion.

The three quantities can come from the instrumentation introduced in Chapter 1. A pool exposes its in-use gauge, a client exposes a duration histogram, and the rate is a counter. Where one is missing, measuring it is usually a smaller task than the load test that would otherwise be needed to answer the same question.

Choosing the Measurements

Figure \(\ref{fig:ch02-boundaries}\) shows the same request measured three ways, and the three answers are all correct for different questions.

For a database connection, occupancy begins at acquisition and ends at release. Acquisition wait occurs before that interval. For a worker assigned to the whole request, occupancy includes the time spent waiting for the database.

A single latency number combines durations that affect different resources. A request that waits 40 milliseconds for a connection and then holds it for 70 has two different durations, and the pool is affected by only one of them.

The scope must match as well. If 400 lookups per second are distributed evenly across four instances, each receives about 100. A calculation for one instance’s pool uses that instance’s rate; fleet-wide capacity must account for all pools and any shared database limit.

Failed work also uses resources. A query that fails after acquiring a connection contributes to connection occupancy until release. A request rejected before acquisition uses no database connection. When measuring a queue, timed-out requests contribute the time they spent waiting.

During stable operation, entries and departures balance over time; during overload, offered requests may arrive faster than work completes. Multiplying the offered rate by mean occupancy then estimates the demand placed on the resource. Actual use is still bounded by its configured capacity.

This distinction prevents an impossible conclusion. A calculation of 54 connections against a pool of 40 means that some offered work must wait, be rejected, or expire. The pool cannot assign 54 connections.

Resources Used by One Request

The same request can occupy several resources for different durations. A short table is often sufficient to identify which ones need further investigation.

Consider one application instance processing 400 requests per second. Every request uses a database connection, and some subsequently make an outbound HTTP call. Measurements taken during a steady interval give the following estimates.

Resource estimates for one illustrative application instance. Each duration covers assignment through release.
Resource Uses/s Mean time Average use Limit
Request workers 400 110 ms 44 64
DB connections 400 70 ms 28 40
HTTP slots 150 80 ms 12 16

The HTTP limit represents concurrent outbound calls. Depending on the protocol and client implementation, several calls may share a network connection, so the configured limit needs to match what the measurement counts.

Suppose mean database acquisition wait increases by 100 milliseconds for every request. The connection is assigned only after acquisition, but each worker waits through that additional interval. At the same throughput, average worker demand would become

\[400 \times (0.110 + 0.100) = 84.\]

The instance has 64 workers, so it cannot sustain that combination of request rate and duration. Requests will queue before obtaining a worker, be rejected, or complete at a lower rate.

This is useful when evaluating a pool increase. The database connection may be the first resource we notice, but a change needs to be checked against the other resources used by the request.

Reducing Connection Occupancy

Before adding capacity, look at what the handler is doing while a connection is assigned to it.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Payload preparation while a connection is assigned.
           The pool API is illustrative.}]
with pool.acquire() as conn:
    payload = build_payload(request)
    result = query_database(conn, payload)

Suppose preparing the payload takes 40 milliseconds and the database operation takes 30 milliseconds. The connection is unavailable to other handlers for approximately 70 milliseconds. If payload preparation uses only request data, it can occur before acquisition.

[
  language=Python,
  caption={Payload preparation before connection acquisition.}]
payload = build_payload(request)

with pool.acquire() as conn:
    result = query_database(conn, payload)

Connection occupancy becomes approximately 30 milliseconds; at 400 operations per second, average connection use falls from 28 to 12. The handler still performs the same payload work. Its response time may be unchanged when there is no queue, but other requests can acquire connections sooner during contention.

This change requires a correctness check. Work that depends on a transaction’s database snapshot or locks cannot be reordered solely to shorten occupancy. The engineer needs to establish which work actually requires the connection.

Workload Variation

A 70-millisecond mean does not show how often a connection is occupied for two seconds. Those longer assignments can affect requests arriving behind them.

An average helps estimate resource use, but customers experience individual requests; their waits depend on the operations already in progress when they arrive.

For example, one workload might use a connection for about 70 milliseconds on nearly every request. Another might use it for 20 milliseconds on most requests and for more than half a second on a small proportion. Both can have the same mean, while producing different acquisition waits.

Compare occupancy distributions when two workloads have the same mean. Occasional two-second assignments can produce different acquisition waits from calls concentrated around 70 milliseconds.

Arrival timing has a similar effect. Four hundred requests spread across a second and four hundred arriving in a short burst can produce the same one-second rate metric. The second workload requires more operations to run concurrently if the requests are to finish promptly.

Mean occupancy can also increase under load. Additional queries may wait on locks, compete for storage access, or take more CPU time. A duration measured at low traffic may therefore be unsuitable for estimating peak capacity.

The practical implication is that an average utilization percentage needs supporting latency measurements. A service operating at 70 percent average use may satisfy its response-time objective with one request mix and miss it with another.

For the next test, the engineers need representative request classes, arrival patterns, and result sizes. The test measures whether the application can process that workload with acceptable waiting and rejection.

Failure Capacity and Shared Limits

Business-as-usual traffic is only one planning condition; the application may also be expected to process that traffic after losing instances.

Suppose ten instances serve 1,000 requests per second with even routing, so each receives about 100 requests per second. After one instance fails, the other nine receive about 111 each; if three fail, the other seven receive about 143 each.

Specify the failure condition behind a capacity estimate. Ten serving instances and seven serving instances give each process different arrival rates, even when the fleet receives the same total workload. That is a 43 percent increase per instance in the second failure case. If the service must continue processing all requests, the test needs to include that rate and the occupancy observed at that rate. Even routing is an assumption to verify. Sticky sessions, partition ownership, and expensive request classes can concentrate work on particular instances.

The expected duration of the failure also affects the design. A bounded queue may accommodate a short burst while replacement instances start. Several hours with fewer instances require a sustainable processing rate or a defined reduction in accepted work.

Related conditions belong in the same test; a restart may combine fewer instances with a cold cache, and a dependency slowdown may cause retries. These combinations describe plausible production events and help the engineers evaluate the recovery plan.

Local Pools and Fleet Capacity

Adding instances also changes the number of connections the application can open. Ten instances with pools of 40 can open up to 400 database connections. If the service has an allocation of 300 database sessions, the local configurations permit more than the shared allocation. Deployment overlap needs to be included. Old and new processes may run together, and a process that has stopped accepting traffic may still use connections while finishing earlier requests.

The team may choose smaller per-instance pools, a fleet-wide limit, or a larger database allocation supported by testing. Adding replicas without revisiting these limits can transfer the problem to the shared database.

::: decision

**Is this fleet sized for the failure it will meet?**

Ten instances share 1,000 requests per second, so each takes about 100. Each instance has a connection pool of 40, and the database allocates the service 300 sessions in total. Your capacity review asks whether the fleet survives the loss of one instance. Which figure settles it?

**Average CPU across the fleet, which sits comfortably below its threshold.**

**The per-instance request rate after redistribution, converted into connection demand.**

**The total configured pool size across the fleet, compared with the database allocation.**

—

B and C answer different halves of the same question, and you need both.

Take B first. Losing one instance leaves nine sharing 1,000 requests, so each receives about 111 rather than 100, an 11 percent increase. At a 70-millisecond mean occupancy that moves average demand per instance from \(100 \times 0.070 = 7\) connections to \(111 \times 0.070 \approx 7.8\). This average is below the pool limit of 40. It still needs a test of bursts and longer connection assignments, as Section \(\ref{sec:ch02-failure-capacity}\) discusses.

Now C. Ten pools of 40 permit up to 400 sessions against a database allocation of 300. The configuration can therefore exceed that allocation even though this example’s average occupancy is lower. The fleet needs a combined limit or smaller local pools, including the extra instances permitted during replacement.

A measures CPU utilization. A handler waiting for a connection can use little CPU, so that measurement does not establish whether the pool allocation is sufficient.

:::

Reading a Load Test

Before interpreting a load test, compare the requested arrival rate with the rate the generator actually delivered.

A load test should help the team select an operating rate and evaluate overload behavior. Its measurements need to account for the work offered, the work completed, and the requests that did not receive the intended result.

Table \(\ref{tab:throughput-knee}\) shows illustrative steady stages for one instance with a 40-connection pool and a bounded acquisition queue. In this example, every lookup that acquires a connection succeeds; the rejected column includes attempts refused or timed out before acquisition.

Illustrative steady load-test stages. Mean use is connection occupancy. Acquisition p95 covers successful acquisitions.
Offered/s Completed/s Rejected/s
(ms)
(ms)
300 300 0 55 2
400 400 0 70 8
480 470 10 80 25
560 440 120 90 80
650 390 260 100 95

At each stage, offered requests are accounted for by completions and rejections, with no sustained increase in unfinished work. If a queue were accumulating, that increase would also need to be recorded.

The last three rows deserve attention. As offered traffic increases, connection occupancy rises and completed throughput falls. The instance spends more time on each completed operation while rejecting a larger proportion of arrivals.

Suppose the application permits an acquisition p95 of 50 milliseconds and at most one percent rejection. The third stage satisfies the latency condition but rejects about 2.1 percent of offered requests. Among the listed stages, the second is the highest that satisfies both conditions.

Further testing between those stages can identify a more precise operating range. Burst and failure tests are still needed before approving it for production. The resource calculation provides a consistency check on the table. At 440 completed lookups per second and 90 milliseconds of mean occupancy, average connection use is 39.6, which fits the configured limit of 40.

A production test would separate acquisition timeouts, execution failures, and cancellations, and it would also record the rate the generator actually sent. A generator that waits for responses before sending more requests can reduce its own arrival rate as the application slows, leaving the intended workload untested.

Queue Wait and Recovery Time

Two questions often arise during overload: how long will a newly accepted request wait, and how long will it take to clear the backlog?

Suppose 1,000 requests are ahead of a new request in a first-in, first-out queue. If workers begin about 500 queued requests per second, the new request waits approximately two seconds before execution, and it still needs its own processing time after that wait. A caller with a one-second deadline would receive no useful result under those conditions.

Clearing the entire backlog takes longer if new requests continue arriving. With 400 new admissions and 500 completions per second, the backlog decreases by 100 requests per second. Removing the 1,000-request backlog takes approximately ten seconds.

Now suppose arrivals rise to 650 per second against the same 500 completions. The queue grows by 150 requests per second, about 1,500 after ten seconds and 9,000 after a minute, and it does not level off for as long as the imbalance lasts (Figure \(\ref{fig:ch02-stability}\)).

The queued request has work ahead of it; recovery also has to account for new work joining behind it. These estimates assume similar request costs, steady processing, and no change in priority. They are useful for deciding whether to admit another synchronous request and how much admission must be reduced during recovery.

If admissions and completions are both 500 per second, their rate difference does not reduce the backlog. Increasing queue capacity would allow more requests to wait without adding processing capacity.

Timeouts require careful accounting too; a timeout that removes a queued request reduces unfinished work. A caller timeout that leaves server-side work executing does not yet release the server resource.

Retries in the Workload Estimate

Retries need to be included in the dependency’s attempt rate. Suppose 400 original requests arrive each second; if 25 percent of first attempts are retried, they add 100 attempts. If 25 percent of those retries receive one final attempt, they add another 25.

Each additional attempt consumes resources, so include the expected attempt count when estimating the work sent to a dependency. The dependency receives

\[400 + 100 + 25 = 525\]

attempts per second once the flow is steady. That is the rate relevant to a dependency that performs work for every attempt. If some attempts are rejected before database acquisition, the database-use rate will be lower than the offered rate.

The slowdown that causes retries may also increase resource occupancy, and both changes belong in the test. Using the original request rate with the slower duration would omit the additional attempts.

Retries at several layers require another check. Three permitted attempts from an upstream caller, each with up to three downstream attempts, can produce nine downstream attempts for one logical operation. The design review therefore needs the attempt limit and the layer responsible for retrying. Chapters 3 and 4 examine which operations can be retried and how deadlines affect that decision.

Comparing Design Changes

We can bring these measurements together when choosing a capacity change. Consider a planning workload of 450 database operations per second with an assumed mean occupancy of 120 milliseconds. That implies average demand of 54 connections, against a pool limit of 40. It describes offered demand rather than a throughput the current pool has achieved.

The team has three proposals:

Alternative designs for the same planning workload. Each estimate depends on the stated assumptions.
Proposed change Average use Evidence needed
Pool from 40 to 80 54 of 80 Database throughput and occupancy at the added concurrency.
Occupancy from 120 ms to 30 ms 13.5 of 40 Correct results and the shorter duration under the planned workload.
Cache serves 90 percent of reads 5.4 of 40 Hit rate, acceptable freshness, and database demand during cache misses or loss.

A larger pool may be appropriate if the database has tested spare capacity and the application’s local limit is the constraint. It may also require a larger database allocation, with additional cost or less capacity available to other workloads. Reducing occupancy may avoid that increase, but the proposed duration needs measurement and a correctness review. A cache reduces database arrivals while introducing freshness and miss-handling requirements; its expected demand applies only while the assumed hit rate is achieved.

The comparison should also include later operations in the request, because completing more database work may send more calls to an external provider. Adding consumers may increase database writes. Any proposal that increases completed throughput needs a check of the dependencies receiving that additional work.

A useful review record can be brief: the proposed workload, the resource limit, the measured or assumed duration, the expected result of the change, and the test that would justify approval. When a request mix or retry policy changes, the service owner can revise those inputs and identify what needs to be tested again.

Summary

The team could diagnose the connection-pool incident more precisely once it separated request throughput from the rate at which each dependency performed work. A page request could involve several database assignments, while a cache hit involved none. The page worker also remained assigned during waits that did not occupy a database connection. Those differences determine which rate and duration belong in a capacity estimate.

Little’s Law provides a useful average, provided the rate and duration refer to the same measured boundary and the observed workload is sufficiently stable. The estimate is a starting point for tests of bursts, variable request costs, lost instances, retry traffic, and time spent in queues. If a larger connection pool merely moves the queue into a saturated database, the application has gained little. If moving computation outside the assigned interval reduces connection occupancy, the same pool can serve more lookups without increasing database sessions.

The calculation also tells the team when to stop admitting work. A queue that grows faster than spare completion capacity can drain will exceed its callers’ deadlines long before it disappears. In Chapter 3, that timing problem acquires a correctness consequence: a remote operation can finish after its caller has given up, and a subsequent attempt may perform the same business action again.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & The candidate pool increase can support the planning workload without unacceptable acquisition waits, rejections, or longer occupancy.
Condition that tests it & Arrival rate, request mix, or resource occupancy exceeds the tested workload.
Constraint or invariant & One instance’s database pool, considered alongside the fleet’s shared database allocation.
Evidence and uncertainty & The planning workload implies average demand above the current pool limit. A larger pool requires database validation.

Occupancy and completed throughput at higher concurrency, after instance loss, and during deployment overlap.
Signal and evaluation window & Measure arrivals, completions, queue time, and resource occupancy over the same observation window.
Control and decision & Test the candidate change. Compare shorter occupancy or fewer database operations if the added concurrency fails the acceptance criteria.
Owner and review trigger & The service owner validates the workload. The database owner confirms the shared allocation. The release owner records acceptance and recovery criteria. Review after the test condition occurs or before expanding exposure.
:::
